# common caller dual-state postmortem

## Original assessment retained in the incident record

This postmortem initially classified the issue as "the same object appearing in two states." The original assessment has not been removed: the entry point returned different current revisions at two points in time, making the call samples from client and extension look as if two copies of the object existed at once. Later checks did not provide enough evidence to overturn that account, so it remains here; but it should not be treated as a confirmed root cause.

The first version retained only the replay divergence and the recovery page. This update records the confirmed display behavior, recovery actions, and what remains unexplained separately, to avoid retroactively using the first normal result after recovery to explain the incident.

## Observed sequence

| Phase | Incident record | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| First replay | The old record and replay did not match; the same object appeared to have two states | Saved the original input and entry point version; stopped repeated retries |
| Narrowing the scope | Some call samples could still produce the original results | Did not treat these normal results as an overall recovery |
| Recovery | source compatibility could be restored | Retained the recovery page; interpolation changes still unknown |
| Record update | The exit entry point could be opened, but kept spinning at the current result | Recorded when it was spinning; did not refresh the page to retry |

"Recovery" here only means that source compatibility could be obtained again at that time. It did not establish that the dual-state display had disappeared, nor did it establish why interpolation changed. The first version linked the two too closely, making it easy to read as though a single cause had already been found; the table retains the original attribution while flagging this conflation.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as client
    participant X as extension
    participant I as Current entry point
    participant R as Original record
    C->>I: Read object state
    X->>I: Read object state
    I-->>R: Different current revisions
    R-->>C: Replay result diverges
    R-->>X: Adaptation result pending investigation
```

The diagram only describes the paths recorded at the time; it does not mean the issue has been localized within the entry point. The original incident record does not contain enough request context to map the call relationships in more detail.

## Additional entry point observations

The SRRA-006 exit entry point check recorded two consecutive observations: the entry point could be opened, but kept spinning at the current result; the time when it was spinning was then recorded, along with an explicit note that the page had not been refreshed to retry. This behavior and the dual-state assessment in the first version were grouped into the same incident because both fell within the scope of caller integration feedback, not because they had been proven to stem from the same change.

SRRA-014: it was later confirmed that this anomaly should retain a separate common-client-integration and timeline, with only a link in the daily report. At one point, the internal results contained the current result, while the normal entry point corresponding to the exit entry point did not. This is a more specific display difference than "two states": the result was visible in one place and absent in another. The old version called them all object state inconsistencies to make investigation easier for the on-call staff, but that umbrella label obscured the differences between the entry points.

SRRA-007: an action that came due was later confirmed to have been sent to the wrong card; it was not part of the same incident as "two record versions zero-result collection status." That action can no longer be used as timing evidence for this incident. Card completion only shows that the checks on that card ended; it must not be reported as the dual-state issue having been eliminated.

## Impact

At the time, the impact was on real call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback involving client and extension. Caller Fang Ke could see the current result in the internal results but not the same result through the normal entry point corresponding to the exit entry point; or, when replaying an old record, get a display that did not match that record. The risk was not that the object data was necessarily corrupted, but that users would treat displays from different entry points as facts from the same point in time.

Screenshots that do not include an account, full version, or run identifier cannot explain why another path worked normally. The screenshot-only secondhand report has not been deleted, but it can no longer support the claim that "the issue has cleared." The last line of green output from the incident is likewise not enough to override the initial divergence.

After recovery, the requirement in SRRA-022 was only to observe the first common · Caller Integration, without using the daily report summary to override the original incident record. This constraint preserved the minimal recovery observation: which entry point recovered, and on which read, must be examined alongside the original record, not inferred from the summary status.

## Actions taken and outstanding issues

Keeping the original record was the right call, because later page states could not replace the input seen at the first divergence. Stopping page refreshes was also reasonable: repeated refreshes would only introduce new read times, not explain why different current revisions were returned at two points in time.

The first version proposed "entry point read timing" as a tentative cause. That assessment should still be treated as a working hypothesis, not a verified attribution. It can explain the difference between two points in time, but not why the result was present in the internal results and absent from the normal entry point, nor the change in interpolation.

SRRA-021: the gap concerning the current revision was handed off to the actual maintainer, while the card itself retained only confirmed material. SRRA-006 also left an entry point cleanup item: follow the action routing for caller integration testing to find who would actually take over, and remove decommissioned groups from the new entry point. Neither of these closed out the root cause; they only served to prevent gaps and obsolete entry points from continuing to get mixed into the same round of integration feedback.

The original record is still at `docs/adj-common/incidents/common-caller-integration-same-object-has-two-states.md`. When reviewing the incident, first distinguish what was recorded in the normal entry point, exit entry point, internal results, and recovery page. Do not replace the full timeline with the current state of just one of those pages.

# common caller dual-state postmortem

This page preserves an outdated incident account. It initially summarized the behavior as "the same object appearing in two states", and attributed the discrepancy to entry points reading different current revision values at two points in time. At the time this assessment helped preserve the discrepancy between replay and the old record as a separate finding, and kept the responders from introducing new inputs through continued refreshes, continued retries; but it reduced the differences between entry points to an object-state issue. The records added later did not provide a single alternative root cause, so the old assessment remains in the body, rather than being rewritten as a seemingly complete current account.

This covers the client, extension call samples and integration feedback in common · Caller Integration. It has its own schedule, maintainer and exit criteria. After the anomaly occurred, the original record, recovery page and unconfirmed causes were preserved separately; they are not the same type of evidence, nor can they substitute for one another.

---

## The incident as preserved in the first version

The first version was very brief, centered on one replay discrepancy: replay differed from the old record. The same object was seen as having two states in the call samples, so the responders focused on when the entry points performed their reads. The original intent of this wording was not to prove that the object internally stored two copies of its state, but to describe the inconsistent displays callers saw at different read locations.

The first version could confirm only three things.

- The original record and the replay result were different.
- source compatibility could be restored.
- Why interpolation changed was still unknown.

Repeated retries were stopped at that point. The reason was straightforward: if a subsequent read changed what was visible on the page, the new result could only show that another read had taken place, not why the first one had deviated. Preserving the original input and the entry-point version was more important than chasing a result that would turn green immediately.

The initial impact assessment was also narrow. It did not say that object data was corrupted, did not say that all callers had failed, and certainly did not include changes in adjacent projects among the causes. All that could be said was: real-world call samples from client and extension could not be reused reliably; the adaptation results had to be viewed together with the entry-point state at the time. This scope was not expanded later.

The first version ended with two gaps: what exactly changed between the two reads; whether the recovery page restored the entry-point display or the object itself. Although several entry-point observations were added later, these two questions did not receive a complete answer.

## The explanation used at the time

> The entry points provided different current revision values at two points in time, so the same object was displayed in two states.

This is the original wording of the old explanation, retained here to show why the old page grouped multiple behaviors under the same incident. At the time it accounted for "the old record and the replay being different", and was also consistent with the responders not immediately finding any object-level changes.

But this statement has clear shortcomings. It did not distinguish between internal results, normal entry points, exit entry points and the recovery page; even when these locations concern the same object, they may display results from different stages. Calling all of them "two states" would lead readers to think that differences between entry points had already been ruled out, when in fact they had not.

The old explanation also failed to explain the change in interpolation. The restoration of source compatibility was once treated as a positive sign, but it was later discovered that this only meant a certain class of compatibility results was available again; it could not substitute for an explanation of the display differences. The first version did not make this distinction, which is the main reason this postmortem was later retained but no longer maintained as current guidance.

## Replay, Save, and Stop

The earliest sequence of operations was to replay first, then save the original record, and then stop retrying. The original record is located at `docs/adj-common/incidents/common-caller-integration-same-object-has-two-states.md`. This file preserves the material provided by the entry point at the time, not a mirror of the page's later state.

After the replay diverged, the team handling the incident did not overwrite the old record with new, normal results. This choice preserved one fact: the divergence did occur in the recorded call samples. It did not preserve the full request context; the first version did not record the account, full version, or run identifier, nor did it record enough detail to reconstruct each call relationship. Therefore, any later claim that "another path works normally" cannot automatically explain the divergence at the time.

During the incident, the time of recovery was also conflated with the time of root cause confirmation. After source compatibility was restored, the page could once again return some results, making it sound as though the incident had ended; yet the change in interpolation remained unexplained. Looking back now, these were two different states: one in which usable results reappeared, and one in which the source of the anomaly had been confirmed. The old record contains only the former, not the latter.

This does not invalidate the decision to "stop retrying". Refreshing the page creates a new read time. If the entry point happens to present a different current revision depending on the read time, even normal results after a refresh cannot tell us whether the original results were replaced, hidden, or simply read at another location.

## Entry Point Differences Added Later

The checks on SRRA-006 revealed more specific observations than those in the first version. The exit entry point could be opened, but it kept spinning when it reached the current results. The recorder then preserved the point in time when it was spinning and did not refresh the page to retry. This observation describes only how the exit entry point behaved during that check: being able to enter does not mean being able to retrieve the current results.

This detail is not quite the same as the "two states" in the first version. The first version emphasized that the same object looked different at two points in time; the observation about the exit entry point emphasized that retrieval of the current results could not proceed past a particular page stage. The two were later included in the same postmortem because both were anomalies exposed by caller integration feedback, but there is no material proving that they were caused by the same internal change.

The scope confirmation on SRRA-014 added another layer: this anomaly needed to retain its own common-client-integration and timeline, with only a link in the daily report. The record states that current results were available in the internal results, but not at the regular entry point corresponding to the exit entry point. The display at the time can therefore be divided into at least two locations: the location of the internal results and the location of the regular entry point. The former had current results, while the latter did not; the exit entry point, meanwhile, kept spinning after entry.

This is more complex than the earlier account, but it does not establish a root-cause conclusion. The existence of internal results does not mean that the same results should have existed at the regular entry point, nor does it mean that the two entry points were reading results from the same point in time. The exit entry point continuing to show a spinner does not mean that the object itself changed either. If the old postmortem directly described these observations as "state synchronization failure", that would go further than the actual material supports; therefore, it was not rewritten that way.

The term "same object" in the old version is still useful: it reminds the integration side not to treat every page result as an unrelated new event. But it can also mislead people into treating outputs from different entry points as data from the same layer. Where the term is retained now, it should be understood as the object being observed for the same call sample, rather than a single storage state that has already been confirmed.

## A record that should not be included in this incident

A due-date action in SRRA-007 was later confirmed to have been sent to the wrong card, and was not part of the same incident context as "two record versions zero-result collection status". This fact may seem minor, but it changes how the timeline can be used: actions on the card can no longer be used to prove what happened in this incident at that point in time.

The fact that the same card later moved from in progress to completed also cannot be used as evidence that the dual states disappeared. Completion means that work on that card stopped in the state it was in at the time, not that the regular entry point, the exit entry point, and the internal results had become consistent. The old version relied fairly heavily on card status to structure the narrative, which made actions without direct records from the incident look like part of the anomaly itself; that approach is no longer applicable.

Keeping this misattribution on record is intended to prevent someone from seeing "completed" in the future and attaching it to the wrong incident timeline. It does not add any new cause of the incident, nor does it change the facts about replay divergence in the initial version.

## Earlier records of the impact window

This incident affected callers' assessment of the results, rather than being a confirmed case of complete unavailability. The adaptation boundaries established by client and extension around actual call samples were disrupted: when using Fang Ke, the current results could be seen in the internal results but not at the regular entry point corresponding to the exit entry point; replaying old records could also produce a different display.

This means that, at the time, saving a screenshot alone did not provide enough explanatory value. A screenshot might capture only the internal results, or only a blank section at the regular entry point; without an account, version, or run identifier, it cannot explain why the other path was working normally, much less whether that path might change at another point in time. The old version's tendency to treat "the last line being green" as a sign of recovery has the same problem.

However, it was not confirmed that all entry points were unavailable. The internal results recorded in SRRA-014 still contained the current results, indicating that at least one observation point did not show the same gap. The initial version did not have enough material to determine whether this was the same read cycle, and could not determine whether it came before or after the spinning at the exit entry point, so it did not treat the internal results as counterevidence or as evidence of recovery.

In this historical record, "recovery" should only be read as limited recovery: source compatibility can be restored, and subsequent observation is limited to the first common · Caller Integration. It is not synonymous with consistency in the object's state, nor is it this page's final conclusion on interpolation.

## Why the recovery page did not replace the incident context

The value of retaining the recovery page is that it marks when a caller result could be observed again; the value of retaining the original record is that it marks when the deviation was observed. Only by keeping the two side by side without overwriting each other can we see that "recovery was possible" and "the cause was unknown" were both true at the same time.

SRRA-022 sets very narrow requirements for after recovery: observe only the first common · Caller Integration, and do not overwrite the original incident context with daily report summaries. This avoids another old misreading: the summarized status in a daily report often looks more complete than the observations from the incident, but it does not include the differences between entry points or when the loading spinner was shown. Writing the summarized results back into the original record would mislead later readers into thinking that the original deviation never occurred.

No further commitment was made to broader verification after recovery. There is no material showing that every client, every extension, or every access path had become consistent again; nor is there any material showing that the original replay could reliably reproduce a normal result. This gap is not because the postmortem omitted a conclusion that would be easy to fill in, but because the incident itself left no observations that could support that conclusion.

The old version contained an implicit inference here: since compatibility had been restored, the dual status was probably just a temporary entry-point display state. This inference was not written out as a separate conclusion, but it influenced how readers understood the recovery page. It is still retained in its historical context, but is no longer carried forward as a current assessment.

## Approaches that did not work

Screenshot-only accounts did not help pinpoint the issue. They lacked the context tied to that specific read, so they could not explain why the internal results differed from the regular entry point or connect the loading spinner to the replay deviation. A screenshot can show what a particular page looked like at a particular moment, but cannot by itself prove the object's state at another entry point.

Treating card completion status as part of the incident timeline did not work either. The accidental send action at SRRA-007 shows that nearby cards may contain similar wording without belonging to the same incident context. Filling in the timeline based on card status would disguise unrelated work actions as an observation.

Relying on refreshes to obtain a normal result did not work either, so there was explicitly no refresh or retry when the exit entry point showed a loading spinner. This stopping point was not a fix; it merely prevented further changes in page state from removing the reference against which the original anomaly could be compared.

The most misleading practice was to turn "the internal results have a current result" into "the object is already normal". The record did not establish that the internal results and the regular entry point were equivalent. The presence of the former only showed that a result was visible there at the time; it did not explain why the regular entry point had no result.

## Previous handling recommendations

The first version recommended initially treating this as a dual status in the display layer and using the timing of entry-point reads as the working hypothesis. At the time, this recommendation helped narrow the scope: it did not directly declare that the object was corrupted, nor did it include neighboring services among the causes. It still explains why records from different times needed to be retained.

But this recommendation cannot account for the entry-point behavior added to the record later. The exit entry point could be opened but showed a loading spinner at the current result, and a result was present internally but absent from the regular entry point, both of which need to be retained separately on the timeline. Forcing them back into "display-layer dual status" would make the original account seem more precise than the evidence supports.

Therefore, this page remains in a somewhat untidy state: the earlier response actions remain, the earlier attribution remains, and the entry-point differences recorded later remain as well. They have not been consolidated into a new, unified explanation. Preserving them this way is closer to the material left at the time than rewriting the account as "identified and restored".

## Follow-up items related to integration boundaries

SRRA-006 include an entry-point cleanup task: follow common · Caller Integration's action routing to find the person actually taking over, and remove groups that have been taken offline from the new entry point. This addresses whether the handoff entry point still points to a usable maintenance path, not the technical attribution of the dual state.

SRRA-021, in contrast, hand off the gap regarding the current revision to the actual maintainer, while the current card retains only confirmed material. Drawing this line avoids piecing together an explanation in the card that goes beyond the evidence from the incident. It does not explain why the current revision differed at the two points in time, nor does it promise that the regular entry point will eventually match the internal result.

The only thing these two tasks have in common is that both address gaps left on the integration side: one cleans up outdated entry points, and the other retains the gap regarding the current revision. Their later existence cannot be used to infer retrospectively that a recovery plan had already been established for this incident.

The decision in SRRA-014 to retain a separate timeline should also continue to be honored. Daily reports can only serve as navigation, not as summaries that replace the incident evidence. The client, extension samples, entry-point displays, and recovery page involved in the incident must remain readable separately; otherwise, "the same object" will once again obscure the actual differences.

## What remains unconfirmed

1. Why the current revision differed between the two reads has not been confirmed.
2. Why the change in interpolation occurred has not been confirmed.
3. It has not been confirmed whether, when source compatibility was restored, the recovery page restored the entry-point display or the compatibility result, or whether the two simply happened to appear at the same time.
4. There is no record of whether the internal result and the regular entry point corresponding to the exit entry point were under the same read conditions.
5. It has not been confirmed whether the exit entry point's change from opening successfully to the current result showing a spinner has the same cause as the earliest replay divergence.

These questions remain in the postmortem not as a request to piece them back together into a presumed root cause, but to mark the limit of the earlier conclusions. The first version saw only the replay divergence; the second version saw differences between entry points; the third version did not obtain enough new incident evidence to bring the matter to a close.

## Review entry point

When you need to check the original anomaly, still start with `docs/adj-common/incidents/common-caller-integration-same-object-has-two-states.md`. First look at what the old records and the recovery page each say, then review the exit entry point observations for SRRA-006, the separate timeline notes for SRRA-014, the current revision gaps for SRRA-021 and the first post-recovery observation for SRRA-022.

This is not a current troubleshooting procedure. The page is still retained because the old records contain a distinction that later summary pages cannot reconstruct: internal results, the normal entry point and the exit entry point should not automatically be treated as repeated displays of the same state. The old version's "entry-point read timing" can still be read as the working hypothesis at the time, but should no longer be cited as a confirmed causal explanation.

Actions not recorded in the original postmortem are not filled in here with speculation.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as client
    participant X as extension
    participant I as Current entry point
    participant R as Original record
    C->>I: Read object state
    X->>I: Read object state
    I-->>R: Different current revisions
    R-->>C: Replay results diverge
    R-->>X: Adaptation results pending investigation
```

# Alternative plan for common callers

At the time, there were two options for integration testing of common-client-integration: continue consolidating through `release gate`, or split `rounding` out of this path. The second option is retained here not because it has already replaced the existing entry point, but because the two processing stages have different failure exits; keeping them under the same gate would leave callers seeing only the combined result.

The source material is at `docs/adj-common/proposals/unadopted-common-caller-integration-route.md`. The two snippets there can be compared, but the available records are not enough to identify the actual callers of `provider bridge`. This gap affects how the split should be interpreted: if the caller already finishes before the bridge, handling `rounding` separately only adds a name downstream and does not create a new integration-testing boundary.

The proposed trial leaves the existing path for `release gate` unchanged. At the current entry point, first record the first branch point before entering `rounding` and the first one after, then compare only the failure exits reached by each of the two stages. The aim is not to classify all failures, but to confirm whether `rounding` really has an independent exit point. Records should stop at the frame boundary; inferences beyond that point are not to be treated as conclusions from the trial yet.

The review requested an additional contrasting input. This input should still pass through the current entry point, but must not follow the original failure route; if it still reaches the same exit before and after the split, the split does not provide enough differentiation. If a contrasting input cannot be prepared, the trial window remains incomplete, and "no difference observed" must not be recorded as a result supporting `release gate`.

The trade-off is clear. Retaining `release gate` means callers only need to check via the original entry point, but the different failure exits will be interpreted together. Splitting out `rounding` allows the boundary to be placed closer to the actual branch point, but requires first verifying the call relationships for `provider bridge` and recording the results of each path. The preference is for the latter, only as a direction for the trial.

There are two rollback triggers: first, after identifying the active callers of `provider bridge`, finding that the split does not cover any independent boundary; second, the contrasting input being unable to distinguish between the two failure exits. If either occurs, do not continue with `rounding` as a separate route. Whether rollback should only restore the old entry point is still undecided; the restoration scope must not be locked down without a conclusion on the callers.

For the follow-up review, just return to that source-material entry point and add the caller and contrasting-input records. If both can support the split, then discuss whether to move this route from trial use into routine integration testing.

# common Caller Entry Point Migration Index

Replacing entry points in common-client-integration is not a directory cleanup. client and extension each have call samples on record, and the failure exits at their adaptation points are not entirely the same; the index therefore retains old entry points, replacement locations, and restoration records by consumer, rather than grouping them by name similarity. This page covers only common · Caller Integration's own schedule, maintenance scope, and exit criteria.

The original index is at `docs/adj-common/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. When opening it, first check whether a record includes the caller, the version used, and the first observed result together. If any of these is missing, the record can still be retained as an old lead, but it cannot be used to mark the old entry point as retired. A replacement entry point appearing in the old directory only shows that someone put it there, not that existing callers have completed the switch.

## A Row in the Index

Each row corresponds to an actual consumer, not a conceptual name. Existing rows should answer at least the following questions:

| Recorded information | What to write | Why it is retained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old entry point | The location the caller actually used before | Restoration needs to return to the same place, not a similarly named location |
| Replacement location | The location to be integrated this time | Lets the next person know which segment is being replaced |
| Consumer | The specific integration side of client or extension | The two types of consumers cannot be merged into one sample just because they use the same name |
| Version and original input | The version used for that call and the unprocessed input | Makes it easier to compare the restored result against the original window |
| First result | What was observed at the first failure, success, or inconsistency | Prevents only cleaned-up screenshots or verbal conclusions from remaining later |
| Restoration record | The result after returning to the old entry point, and whether the original input was reused | Distinguishes "the switch was not completed" from "the replacement entry point itself needs further investigation" |

The table does not treat "migrated" as an independent fact. It can only be supported when the replacement location remains valid, the corresponding caller confirms it is usable, and a historical lookup can still find the original record, all at the same time. If only the replacement location has been filled in, the status remains migration in progress; if the old entry point can be restored but the new entry point's result cannot be reproduced, the status also remains migration in progress.

An early draft treated `source compatibility` as an old path that could continue to be used, and viewed `interpolation` as a replacement direction that could be split out separately. This judgment came from the different failure exits of two segments in the index, not from a uniform classification of all entry points. The draft did not identify the current callers of `permutation`, nor did it answer whether rolling back after the split would restore only the old entry point. Those two unresolved records remain in the index and cannot be automatically closed by samples added later.

```text
Old entry point: source compatibility
        │
        ├── Retain the original call samples and restoration location
        │
        └── Split-out trial: interpolation
                    ├── packed lanes
                    └── rounding
```

`packed lanes` and `rounding` in the diagram are names used in the trial records to distinguish the results of two segments. They are not another entry point hierarchy, nor do they mean that every caller must go through one of them. If a consumer does not appear in the corresponding records, do not fill in a path for it just to make the diagram complete.

## Migrating Away from the Old Entry Point

Start with callers that are still using it. For a given client or extension, copy its old entry point, version, and original input; attach the first result as-is below that row. Here, "as-is" means the result seen at the time of failure and the call state at that moment, not a summary rewritten later for easier reading. A successful result after restoration must not overwrite the first failure either; the two need to remain side by side.

Next, connect only this consumer to the replacement location. During the trial, do not replace other entry points at the same time, and do not treat behavior observed in another extension as this consumer's result. Use the same consumer, the same input, and the same observation window for comparisons; change only one condition per comparison. This keeps changes in `rounding` out of the records for `packed lanes`, and prevents other adaptation actions from obscuring the restoration results for the old entry point.

Once the replacement location works for the first time, immediately make another call and record the second call's state. Keep the first result, the error details, and the second call's state near the same row. If the second state is inconsistent with the first, first restore the old entry point for that consumer, then check once more using the original input. Restoration is not a final conclusion proving that the migration failed; it simply brings subsequent investigation out of a mixed state and back to the original entry point.

If a consumer still shows abnormal behavior after restoration, do not rewrite that behavior as "the old entry point is unavailable". First check whether restoration returned to the old entry point recorded in this row, rather than to a location that merely has the same or a similar name in the directory. After confirming the return to the original entry point, retain the restoration result; keep the replacement location's records as well, for comparison with later integration feedback.

When the result of `rounding` is inconsistent with the original window, the handling order in the index is: restore that consumer's old entry point, check once more using the original input, then append the restored result beside the original failure window. Do not delete the record of the inconsistent run. A green result obtained later only shows that the call after restoration was different; it cannot change what actually happened during the initial trial.

The trial of `packed lanes` follows the same recording method, but does not share a result row with `rounding`. The failure exits of the two segments were the reason for deciding to split `interpolation`; if a caller later encounters a problem in only one segment, it should still be described in that segment's row, rather than moved to an abstract overall "entry point migration" item.

## Old Records and Restoration Records

The index retains some incomplete old notes. They are still useful: they can show which entry point an investigation originally started from, and indicate that a consumer already existed before the replacement. However, notes whose caller or version cannot be traced back should explicitly remain marked as outdated. Outdated does not mean deleted; it means that the row cannot be used to determine whether the current migration is complete.

Earlier wording raised the question of "restoring only the old entry point". This is no longer treated as the default action. Restoration needs to consider whether this consumer has already integrated the split-out `interpolation`, and whether comparable results can still be obtained using the original input after restoration. If only the old location in the directory has been restored, but not the location the actual call went through, this round can only be recorded as restoration unconfirmed.

Place the restoration record after the original failure window, rather than creating a separate success record that appears independent. This makes the relationship between the same caller's replacement location, old entry point, and repeat call visible. Integration feedback also goes here: it can describe what the caller encountered at the adaptation boundary, but cannot replace the original input or the first result.

Do not substitute "the new entry point exists" for restoration checks. Maintenance of a row can truly end only when: the replacement location remains accessible, the corresponding caller confirms the switch, and the old record can still be found through the index. Unless all three conditions are met at the same time, the old entry point stays in the index; this both allows later restoration and tells the next migration batch where the previous work stopped.

## Migration Batches

Batches progress by caller, not by the number of files in the directory. A batch may contain only one client or only one extension; its boundaries are determined by the actual integration samples in that batch, adaptation feedback, and whether the old entry point can be restored. Names without samples are not added just to fill out a batch.

When starting a batch, first retain the original location in the old entry point column, then fill in the replacement location being tried in this batch. After replacement is complete, add the first result and the second call's state. If restoration is needed during the process, append the restoration record first, then decide whether to pause that consumer. Pausing does not prevent other confirmed consumers from continuing their migrations, but other consumers' successful results cannot be used to close this consumer's case.

Batches do not share a "completed" label. A working replacement location for client does not mean that extension's adaptation boundary has passed validation; a normal restoration for extension cannot be backfilled as a success for client either. The index uses this narrower recording approach to keep caller results traceable, rather than compressing all integration feedback into one aggregate status.

`permutation` remains an exception. The old draft only recorded that no current caller had been found, and no follow-up material supports marking it as migrated or deprecated. It remains among the items not yet checked back, to prevent anyone from misreading the absence of samples as the absence of consumers. Once an actual consumer is found, create a corresponding row and start with the old entry point, version, and original input, rather than marking it complete directly from its current blank state.

## Connections to Related Records

SRRA-003 documented the problem of missing intermediate records in the old entry point migration, and noted that the card's "current result" is an old result. When handling these rows, retain the old result as a historical window and write later additions beside it; do not replace the old text in the card with the new result. SRRA-010 are used to append restoration results, with the requirement that the original failure window and object not be overwritten. SRRA-017 retain access to rechecking the public entry point; local results are used only to locate issues and do not replace revalidation in the public environment.

These cards only help locate the corresponding work records. The index itself still relies on one row per caller: the old entry point, replacement location, original input, first result, and restoration result must be readable in the same place. Changes to card status do not replace these details, nor do they determine whether an old entry point can be removed.

## Loose Ends Still Under Maintenance

Some integration feedback only describes the adaptation boundary and is not sufficient to establish the state of the replacement location itself. When encountering this kind of feedback, first attach it within the relevant client or extension row and indicate whether it concerns the old entry point or the replacement location; do not infer another consumer's migration conclusion from it.

Similarly named bypass paths are not automatically included in this index. What is recorded here is the call samples already observed by common-client-integration, not an entry point directory for the entire workspace. If a bypass path later needs migration, retain its own old entry point and restoration results, then determine whether its replacement location is the same as one already listed here.

The endpoint for maintaining this page is also specific: callers still in use have replacement locations and restoration records, old notes that cannot be traced back remain explicitly marked as outdated, and a blank is no longer treated as a conclusion for `permutation`. Other entry point names without supporting samples remain outside the index.

# neoforge compatibility catalog exit checklist

During the window, check only three things: the exit action, the last visible result, and adj-neoforge's own exit action. This checklist does not determine whether the release succeeded; that still requires separate sign-off from the responsible owner. Before starting, open `docs/adj-neoforge/release/neoforge-compatibility-catalog-exit-window-checklist.md`; do not substitute a similarly named record.

## Before the window opens

- [ ] Confirm that the target is still `neoforge-compatibility-catalog`, and write the intended exit action next to the window record. If the action is not tied to that target, do not continue the checks.
- [ ] Record the original location of the last visible result, or a verbatim excerpt. The only requirement here is that it remain visible at review time; do not infer from it that the release has completed.
- [ ] List adj-neoforge's exit action separately. It may happen at the same time as the catalog object's exit action, but do not treat the latter as complete just because the former has been recorded.

## During the window

1. Check the record to verify whether the exit action has been carried out. If all you see is a plan, discussion, or to-do item with no corresponding action, stop here; do not fill in the record as though the exit had happened.
2. Review the last visible result. If it is missing, cannot be located, or does not match this target, retain the window record and stop further cleanup.
3. Check whether adj-neoforge's exit action is independently visible. If that action still has not appeared, the window can remain incomplete; do not use the catalog-side result to sign off on it.
4. When all three check out, mark only this checklist's checks as complete. Hand the release result back to the responsible owner to handle; do not add a release conclusion here.

## Stopping work

If any item is unrecorded, the target name cannot be matched, or the last visible result is no longer visible, do not clean up or mark the window as complete. First retain the existing records and original entry point, then wait until the exit action or result is restored before checking again.

Recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment, so do not treat recovery as the default step after stopping. If recovery is needed, the person responsible for that release should first confirm whether to carry it out; this checklist only retains the verification status for the exit window.

## Retention

After the window ends, the record should show which exit action was checked, where the last visible result was retained, and whether adj-neoforge's action has appeared. Mark anything uncertain as unconfirmed; do not use release sign-off in place of confirmation. If the entry point's contents change later, review them through the same path, then add a new window record.

# neoforge Compatibility Directory Alternative Proposal

This page retains one of the organizational approaches that neoforge-compatibility-catalog once considered but later did not adopt. It was originally kept because `channel order` placed the two relationship entries in the same queue, while field records showed that they would exit through different failure paths. The thinking at the time was straightforward: set `stable ties` aside, and directory readers could see the two exit paths without having to infer them from the order.

Only a few options were written down at the time.

> Continue along `channel order`, or split out `stable ties`. Don't change the entry point yet; restore the old entry point on error.

This original assessment remains because it explains why the proposal came about; it is not a step that can be executed directly afterward. In particular, the phrase "restore the old entry point" did not account for the state left behind by the exit action. The current callers of `normal identity` had not all been identified either, and whether splitting would change the relationship visible to callers had not been fully checked in the first place.

During the second pass, the candidate implementation was called `packed lanes`. The intent was not to replace directory names or use this as an opportunity to adjust display labels, but to divide the relationships originally placed side by side in a single sequence into two channels that could be compared. The benefit was that, after an error, the corresponding channel could be revisited; the cost was just as direct: if callers treated the original order as stable input, the additional hierarchy inside the directory might not be transparent to them.

The observation method drafted at the time called only for retaining the same input, the version used, and the first visible directory result. It did not treat a single green run as a pass, or a mere label change as a result. If `rounding` could not be restored after exit, the trial should stop. Here, "stop" means stopping further rollout of the candidate ordering, not claiming that the directory had been restored; the old entry point, old task, and cache might each still have state left behind.

The records after the window closed made this distinction concrete. In SRRB-003, the current result had not been updated, and the old task still occupied its slot. What this first disproves is the optimistic claim that "switching back to the entry point is enough to wrap up"; it is not enough to attribute the issue to `packed lanes`. SRRB-004 requires preserving the time when the window ended, then checking whether the current entry actually read the old cache or the old task; the two cases cannot be handled together.

SRRB-008 documents a cold-start difference. The processing sequence was limited to clearing the local cache and rerunning the current entry; the shared cache was not included in this route. This boundary matters: if the shared cache is cleared as well, the results seen afterward can no longer be compared with the original records. The early draft wrote "rerun succeeded" too close to "recovery complete"; that wording is withdrawn here.

Another blocker came from the maintenance entry. SRRB-009 found that the records on the two sides were inconsistent, so the only option was to first compare the generation commands and timestamps, then stop at the first divergence. The exit entry in the latter half was not completed during the shift, so there is no complete exit chain on which to base a fixed procedure. SRRB-014 also preserved a more basic issue: the original command arguments were missing; the arguments added later should be listed separately and cannot be backfilled as conditions that had already been verified at the time.

Therefore, this route was never adopted—not because the directory split was proven to be inevitably wrong, but because several prerequisites it depended on did not all hold at once: the caller scope had not been fully checked, the exit action was not completed, the source of the old value after the window had not been distinguished, and the original command was incomplete. Collapsing these gaps into a conclusion that it had "already been rolled back" would obscure the difference in exit paths that the proposal was originally meant to address.

Looking back, the split in `stable ties` can still serve as a reading clue during troubleshooting; `packed lanes` is merely the candidate implementation name from that time. It should not be treated as the current directory structure, nor should it be used to replace the current entry. If someone needs to trace the original context, start at `docs/adj-neoforge/proposals/unadopted-neoforge-compatibility-catalog-route.md`, then review separately the local records for SRRB-003, SRRB-004, SRRB-008, SRRB-009, and SRRB-014.

The unresolved issues did not disappear when the proposal was withdrawn: the gap in the caller list for `normal identity` remains, and the location of the first divergence between the two maintenance entries has not been recorded on this page. The latter needs to be reassessed after the command arguments are recovered; this old proposal cannot be used to fill in the answer.

# buildSrc Release Automation Entry Point Migration Index

This index preserves the migration guidance as it stood at buildsrc-release-automation. It covers only entry point changes involving `.github/workflows`, the build queues formed by release, artifact versions, and rollback windows; schedules and consumer records for peripheral projects are still maintained in their respective locations. The index file is at `docs/adj-buildsrc/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Some old locations are no longer easy to trace directly, so this page must not be treated as up-to-date release notes.

> Old note: As soon as a replacement location appears in the directory, we can start removing the old entry point.

That sentence has not been removed. It reflects the judgment made when the directory was first organized, but is no longer a completion criterion. Adding a row to the directory only shows that someone has added a replacement location. It does not show that the release queue has moved over from the old location, much less that callers still using it have switched.

```text
Old entry point ──> Original release queue ──> Artifact version
  │                       │
  │                       └── Can still return to the old entry point within the rollback window
  │
  └── Replacement location ──> Trial callers
```

## The two kinds of locations in the index

"Old entry point" refers to a location that can still be found in the index and may be used by existing callers. "Replacement location" refers to the location intended to take over for that consumer; it may be in `.github/workflows`, or it may just be a listing alongside the release process. Keep separate records even when their names are similar; do not merge locations with the same name into a single migration batch.

Each record must retain at least three pieces of local information: the old entry point's location in the index, the replacement location's location in the index, and the consumers that can be confirmed. Do not write artifact versions and rollback windows next to the location names; record them separately with that release. Otherwise, someone consulting the index later may mistake the rollback conditions for an old version for properties of the new entry point.

Keep old entry points that have no consumers listed in the index. These entries were previously marked "safe to clean up"; they are now marked "pending confirmation": missing caller information does not mean there are no callers, only that this material did not identify them. This change is not proof that the old location is valid.

## Record sequence for a migration

First, select one caller using an old entry point that can still be identified. Before switching it over, record that caller's release queue, artifact version, and the rollback window allowed at the time. There is no need to fill in every historical version here; the record only needs to let a later rollback be matched to the same batch of artifacts.

Next, switch only this caller to the replacement location. Do not modify another old entry point at the same time, or combine results from multiple queues into a single migration record. Once the replacement location is handling the caller, check whether that caller can still locate the same batch of release artifacts; if the artifact version has moved to a different batch, record the switch and the version change separately. Do not use this as grounds to assert that the entry point migration caused the difference.

Keep the old entry point at this stage. It is not meant to be a permanent parallel track; it gives consumers a clear return point within the rollback window. The "old" label in the index does not mean the entry point can be deleted immediately, either. Mark the entry as complete on this page only after its actual consumers no longer depend on it, the replacement location can be found again, and the corresponding rollback window has been handled for that release batch.

## Handling a rollback

If a rollback is needed after connecting the replacement location, first restore the old entry point for that caller, then verify its release queue and artifact version. Do not substitute another caller's success record for this rollback, or skip the restore step just because the new location is still in the directory.

After the rollback, keep the entry for the replacement location used in this attempt, and state that it did not become this caller's entry point. This lets later maintainers distinguish between "replacement location never tried" and "tried, then returned to the old entry point." Early versions only said "restore the old entry point," without bringing the queue and artifact version back into the same record, making it easy to mix up two releases when reviewing old material. This page preserves that gap; it does not invent version information that was not recorded at the time.

## Parts that are still outdated

This page originally treated `.github/workflows` as the common destination for all replacement locations. When organizing the records, this can only serve as a starting point for lookup, not a determination of where each old entry point has migrated. The relationships between release queues, artifact versions, and rollback windows need to be recorded for each specific consumer; the index only puts old locations, replacement locations, and the callers still using them side by side.

Maintainers and exit criteria are not covered in detail on this page; see DOC-42 for the relevant mapping. The old entry point names and notes about locations that can no longer be traced are retained here so that later maintainers do not mistake broken historical locations for locations that never existed.

# Nightly Rendering Lane Decision Record

This record preserves a wrap-up decision for Lumen Forge on the nightly render lane; it is not an explanation of every rendering adjustment made afterward. The initial draft only said "keep the entry point, defer the window," which could easily be read during handoff as two overly simple conclusions: either the old entry point had been confirmed as a long-term fixture, or the window had been rejected. Both interpretations went beyond the decision made at the time.

There were not many options on the table for review. The first was to continue using the current color-interop entry point so that existing callers could remain unchanged for now; the second was to adjust around the compatibility window and shift the coordination focus away from the old entry point. The latter appeared more focused and more like cleanup that could be completed in the same round. The problem was that the discussion contained no material showing what path would carry forward use of the old entry point after the window adjustment, nor which adjacent modules had already been checked against that change.

This round therefore chose the first option: the current color-interop entry point remains in place, and the window adjustment can continue to be discussed, but it does not take on responsibility for replacing the entry point. Here, "retain" only means that the old entry point continues to be available as a reversible option; it does not mean that it has been redefined as the long-term center, nor that any caller has completed compatibility handling. The decision accepts the cleanup cost of keeping the entry point visible, rather than removing an existing path while the boundary remains unclear.

The initial draft framed the window issue too narrowly. The working assumption at the time was that, as long as the window was tightened, the impact on interop could be contained within the nightly render lane. This assumption was not retained later, but it was not deleted: it explains why some people argued for switching directly. After review, the defensible statement is narrower—the window can be an adjustment target; whether it was sufficient to replace the current entry point had not been determined at the time.

## The Verification Starting Point at the Time

The material starts at the following location:

`neoforge/src/main/java/net/caffeinemc/mods/sodium/neoforge/render/FluidRendererImpl.java`

The review traced back from this location and from the render, forge, and color call names. It provides a reviewable source entry point, not a complete color-interop ownership map. The benefit of starting here is that the discussion can stay grounded in objects that are already visible; the limitation is equally direct: a single file cannot declare the impact scope on behalf of callers, much less turn a local check into a complete loader compatibility conclusion.

The meeting required cross-module changes to first be grounded in a reproducible source entry point, probe output, or commit context before the boundary was determined. This was not intended to turn every discussion into a tracing exercise, but rather reflected that whether the entry point should be retained, what the window is expected to change, and which modules will be affected are three different questions. They may arise in the same round, but none of them can answer the other two.

After review, the coordination record was organized around this distinction. The entry point is the lookup anchor; the window is the adjustment target still under discussion; the handoff is the transaction that lets callers know the old path remains retractable. Discovering a new call relationship at the entry point does not automatically approve the window adjustment. A new proposal for the window should not, in turn, rewrite facts about the entry point that have already been checked.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Current color-interop entry point] --> B[Retained this round]
    B --> C[Old entry point remains retractable]
    D[Window adjustment] --> E[Continue discussion]
    F[Source entry point, probe output, commit context] --> G[Cross-module change boundary]
```

The lines in the diagram only represent the handling relationships among the objects in this record. The window is not drawn as a replacement for the old entry point because that replacement relationship was precisely what could not be confirmed at the time.

## Approaches Compared

| Approach | What could be discussed based on the material available then | Cost left behind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current color-interop entry point | The existing entry point can be traced directly, and the old path remains available | Subsequent window cleanup must also account for the old entry point |
| Replace the entry point with the window adjustment | The handling could appear to be concentrated on the window | The exit method, handoff path, and cross-module impact were not specified |

The second option was not selected as this round's outcome. This was not because window adjustment was necessarily inappropriate, but because it required several prerequisites that were not available at the time: the conditions under which the old entry point would exit, who would take over existing usage after the exit, and which modules had been rechecked under the new relationship. If any one of these is missing, treating the window as a replacement gives the coordinator a switching request that appears clear but is not actually reversible.

Retaining the entry point also has a cost. Some people were concerned that the nightly render lane would consequently retain two narratives at once, making subsequent cleanup slower. That concern is reasonable and was not rejected during review. The actual choice was simply that the two risks could not be treated as equivalent: keeping the entry point visible creates cleanup pressure; removing it without sufficient material loses the option of returning to a checked path. This round accepts the former risk first.

Another proposal was that, since a source location was already available, the entire color-interop chain should be finalized at the same time. The review did not accept this expansion. The entry point, probe output, and commit context are sufficient to support a local discussion, but they do not automatically provide every call relationship. Extending the decision to modules not covered by this material would make the document look complete while obscuring the scope that has actually been confirmed.

## Old Wording That Has Been Corrected

The working sentence in the initial draft was:

> If the window can stably cover the nightly render lane, the old entry point can exit in the same round.

This statement no longer applies. It conflated "the window can continue to be adjusted" with "the window is already capable of taking over for the entry point." The later review changed it to a narrower treatment: while the judgment on the window side has not been established, coordination can continue from the current entry point; the window has not thereby earned the qualification to replace the entry point.

This correction should not be read as a new long-term rule. It only explains why this round did not switch directly. If later material does change the relationship between the entry point and the window, the exit conditions, handoff path, and impact scope must still be compared again; the phrase "exit in the same round" cannot be treated as the default arrangement simply because it appeared in the old record.

The initial draft also contained an inaccurate implication that retaining the old entry point meant callers no longer needed to recheck. That is not the case. Retaining the entry point means callers are not forced to switch routes immediately solely because of the window discussion, but whether a caller falls within the already confirmed scope must still be determined from the material left by this round. Keeping the entry point solves the reversion choice; it does not mean the compatibility work is finished.

## What Must Remain for Handoff

When the coordinator takes over, they should be able to find three specific records: which entry point the trace-back landed on; what scope the window adjustment is expected to touch; and under what circumstances the old entry point can still serve as a reversion option. Previously, these three items were combined into one "aligned" note, making every mention of the old entry point seem like a new request for technical judgment. Once separated, no new material on the window side means the entry-point check does not need to be reopened; a new relationship on the entry-point side does not require assuming that the window has been approved.

This does not prescribe a uniform handoff format. The material different modules can provide is not the same. What must be retained is the object underlying the judgment, rather than turning the coordination note into an abstract state. In particular, when someone is preparing to describe the window adjustment as a replacement action, they should at least be able to identify the old entry point's exit plan and the verification scope for the relevant modules; otherwise, it should continue to be treated as a trial.

For the handoff related to the loader compatibility window, see DOC-44. That page handles the specific handoff for the compatibility window and does not replace the decision background on this page. It is mentioned here only to prevent "the window is still under discussion" from being misread as "the handoff is complete," and to prevent later arrangements on the other page from being projected back into the material conditions of this review.

## Questions Left at the Boundary

If the window adjustment changes callers' expectations of the entry point, the coordination record needs to distinguish a trial that remains retractable from a path that has already been replaced. This round only established that the former can be retained; there was not enough content at the time to state the latter concretely. This question was not split off separately because it directly determines whether the old entry point can continue to serve as a reversion option.

The date and fixed threshold for the old entry point's exit are also not given here. There was no material at the time on which to hard-code them. Filling the blank with a default threshold would disguise a coordination arrangement as an already completed technical decision. If new calls, probe output, or commit context are added later, first determine whether they change the relationship between the entry point and the window, then decide whether the exit needs to be discussed again.

Therefore, this old record can still explain why the nightly render lane did not switch directly: the window approach was not permanently rejected, and the current color-interop entry point was not declared the only option. What it leaves behind is a smaller decision—preserve the retractable old entry point and refuse to let an evidence-insufficient window judgment carry a larger cross-module commitment. The initial draft's interpretation that "the window has already contained the impact" is outdated; checking from a reproducible entry point remains the working starting point left by this review.

# on-call rotation window discrepancy retrospective

This is a field record from an on-call window. The outcome observed during the window did not match the original plan. We first handled what would let the shift continue, but the cause was not closed out at the time. The actual impact, coordinator, and reversible old entry were added later. These points are retained so that "recovered" does not obscure the fact that the investigation is still incomplete.

### Timeline

- **Window start**: Entered the on-call rotation according to the original plan. No separate anomaly was flagged initially; the expectation in the record was still to proceed as planned.
- **Initial discovery**: The observable outcome diverged from the plan. We first checked what had actually happened rather than immediately attributing the issue to a particular call name or person.
- **Temporary recovery**: During the shift, we reverted to the reversible old entry so processing could continue. This relieved the immediate blockage but did not prove that the old entry was the source of the discrepancy.
- **Review**: We compared the API diff left at the time and reviewed the relevant locations by following the call name. The review only shows what was checked at the time; it cannot, by itself, determine where the impact began.
- **Window close**: The actual impact and coordinator were added to the record, with the cause noted as unknown. The recovery action and the cause assessment were not combined into a single conclusion.

### Judgments retained from the time

At one point, attention was focused on the call relationship, with the assumption that the location indicated by the call name might be the ownership boundary. After further comparison, there was insufficient basis for that judgment, so it remains only a working hypothesis. The discrepancy can be confirmed as having occurred between the on-call plan and the observable outcome, but the existing record cannot distinguish whether the first problem was in plan handoff, call handoff, or another step.

The scope of the impact was also not fully quantified. What can be confirmed is that the shift required renewed coordination, could not continue through the original entry for a period, and used the old entry to restore work. There is no evidence that all runtime processes failed, nor that all other paths were functioning normally after recovery. The API diff shows which changes were examined during the review, but it does not establish the complete user-side or runtime impact.

### Still unconfirmed

The time when the discrepancy first appeared has not been confirmed, nor has the mapping between the call name and the ownership location, or whether the temporary recovery changed subsequent results. The old entry remains in this historical record because it was the fallback actually used at the time; this does not mean it has become part of the current on-call plan. If this is reviewed again, start by comparing the actual outcome from the window with the API diff; do not infer the root cause from the successful recovery.
